I thought I'd talk about a few of the books I've read or been reading lately. One of them is the essay by C. S. Lewis, "On Stories," published in 1947. Lewis is the author of the Narnia series of young-adult fantasy. In this essay Lewis talks about the nature of the story. He's a little vague at the opening of the essay as to exactly what he means by "the story" but I gathered that he is talking about the emotional atmosphere that certain topics in stories create in the minds of readers, which in Lewis's opinion transcends the mere series of events in the plot, and even transcends character exposition. He seems to have an opinion similar to that of H. P. Lovecraft, who in his own stories cared nothing about human interrelations but was almost wholly concerned with generating what Lovecraft called "cosmic horror," that feeling of existential dread and sense of unreality that creates a deep unease in the mind. Lewis wasn't specifically writing about cosmic horror, but about all the similar emotional effects of atmosphere, which he called "poetic" in nature, that elevate a story above a simple narrative of sequential events. The essay is not a long read. Fan of Narnia might want to give it a try.

Another book I'm working on is Jerome K. Jerome's autobiographical My Life and Times, published in 1926. Jerome is the author of the well known and well loved humorous Edwardian work Three Men In A Boat -- To Say Nothing of the Dog. in his Life and Times he talks about his childhood, his writings and his literary connections. It is a fascinating, if somewhat chaotic, peek into ordinary life in late Victorian and Edwardian times. Jerome's writing style is stream of consciousness, or close enough to it that there is no difference. Whatever pops into his mind, he sets down immediately without regard for paragraph breaks. He hops from one topic to another like Twain's celebrated jumping frog. But he personal anecdotes are golden. He actually met Mark Twain, along with Oscar Wilde ("we all avoided him"), J. M. Barrie, Walter de la Mare, Bernard Shaw, and a host of other literary giants. Jerome was also heavily involved in the London stage scene, and has countless tidbits to drop about the great actors and producers and playwrites of the age. For example, Sarah Bernhardt was reduced to tears at a gathering of dramatic lumenaries because nobody made a fuss about her -- she fled before the end of the evening in a handsome cab. I loved his little dissertation on the development of the bicycle. You won't find a more fascinating insight into this period of English history.

Another book I recently finished is T. E. D. Kline's story collection, Dark Gods (Viking, 1985). This is a set of four longish stories -- "Petey," "Children of the Kingdom," "Black Man with a Horn," and "Nadelman's God." Kline is a fine writer. He reads easily and knows how to develop character. BUT ... (there's always the "but" in this sort of sentence construction, isn't there?) I didn't really enjoy his stories all that much. They have no effective endings. The buildup is great. It's atmospheric, ominous, detailed ... and then nothing. The air is let out of the balloon. No resolution. No explanation. No exciting climax. The reader is supposed to be content with vague intimations of great evils. Well, I wasn't content, not at all. I'm in the process of reading Kline's novel The Ceremonies (Bantam, 2011) and I noticed that after I had read around 200 pages into the novel, nothing of any consequence at all had taken place. Nothing. Kline apparently thinks we're going to be satisfied to read about the personal minutiae of his petty and not very likeable characters. Well, he's wrong. I learned a lot more than I ever wanted to know about planting corn with a pointy stick. Maybe there are great things ahead for me in the second half of this novel, but the first half overwhelmed me with ennui.

I guess I'll stop here. I hope some of you have found some interest in these few remarks.
